Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Ravi was twenty-nine years old when he came to his first appointment, though he said it felt like he'd been living the past three years in a kind of fractured time. He was a painter—commercial work mostly, the kind that paid steadily if not generously—and his wife Priya had finally insisted he see someone after he'd snapped at her over a spilled cup of coffee with a violence in his voice that scared them both. That incident had happened on a Tuesday morning in their kitchen in Jersey City, ordinary light coming through the window, and Ravi couldn't quite explain why her reaching for a dish towel had made him feel like the walls were closing in.

The mugging had occurred three years earlier, when Ravi was twenty-six, on a November evening when he was walking home from a supply run. He'd taken a shortcut through an underpass near the PATH station—a route he'd walked a hundred times. Two men had come at him from behind; he remembered the sudden weight of hands on his shoulders, the shock of being pushed against the concrete wall. His wallet was gone in seconds. But what stayed with him, what he couldn't quite piece together, was the middle part. There were fragments: a fist near his face, his own voice saying something he couldn't now recall, the smell of wet concrete and something chemical. The rest was fog. He'd been knocked down, that much he knew. He'd gotten up and walked home, his shirt torn, his hands scraped raw. He'd told Priya he'd fallen.

For months afterward, Ravi had slept poorly. The nightmares started almost immediately—vivid, formless things where he was being cornered, his limbs heavy and unresponsive. Waking from these dreams meant his heart would race for an hour. His body wouldn't settle. Even now, three years later, he'd jolt awake at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, the dream dissolving but leaving behind a residue of dread that colored the entire next day. Priya learned not to touch him when he first woke. During the day, he found himself unable to sit still for long; his leg would bounce, his fingers would drum against surfaces, as if his body was perpetually braced for something to happen. When Priya tried to hold his hand while watching television, he'd often pull away, not from rejection but from a need to keep his limbs free, ready to move.

At work, Ravi had become hypervigilant in ways that made the job harder. He worked on residential and commercial properties, often alone or with one other painter, and he found himself constantly aware of who was in the building, where exits were, whether someone might come up behind him. On scaffolding, he'd catch himself scanning the street below, watching for movement, for threat. His concentration fractured. A job that should have taken three days would stretch to four because he'd lose focus, his mind cycling back to the mugging, or jumping at the sound of footsteps on a stairwell. Last month, a client had complained that Ravi seemed distracted, that he'd painted over a section twice because he wasn't paying attention. The contractor had started assigning him smaller jobs, shorter timelines—the kind that paid less. Ravi knew his reputation was slipping, that people were beginning to see him as unreliable, but he couldn't seem to stop the vigilance or the way his mind would suddenly blank out.

The intrusive memories came without warning—a man's voice behind him in a hardware store would trigger a sudden flash of the underpass, the pressure of hands, though the rest remained opaque to him. He'd try to reconstruct what happened, to fill in the missing pieces, but the harder he pushed to remember, the more the memory scattered. There was guilt attached to this fragmentation, though he couldn't articulate why. Part of him wondered if he'd done something to provoke the attack, if there was something he'd failed to do to stop it, something he'd forgotten. The incomplete picture felt like his own failure. Over the three years, Ravi had begun to believe that people couldn't be trusted—not in any absolute way. His wife was an exception, or so he told himself, though even that felt fragile. He'd stopped going to the local deli where he used to buy coffee, stopped taking walks in the neighborhood. He'd withdrawn from his small circle of friends, convinced that their concern was performative, that no one could really understand or help. When Priya suggested he meet her sister for dinner, he'd refused with an anger that surprised them both. The isolation had compounded; he felt set apart now, marked by something the mugging had done to him that others couldn't see but that he carried like a wound that wouldn't close.

His body remained in a constant state of readiness. His shoulders ached from the tension. His jaw was tight. He slept with the bedroom door locked and the lights dimmed but not off. Priya had stopped trying to get him to relax; his irritability had become a feature of their marriage, something they both moved around carefully. When he finally came to the appointment, Ravi said he wasn't sure what help would look like. He just knew that he couldn't keep living like this, that something had broken in him that November night three years ago, and that he was afraid—though of what exactly, he couldn't say. What frightened him most was that the fog around the middle of the attack might never lift, that he'd be forever unable to understand what had happened to him, and that this not-knowing would continue to hollow him out from the inside.
